explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This is a standalone CLI tool (“go-blueprint”) written in Go.  
   - Its purpose is to generate scaffolded Go projects with optional integrations (HTTP frameworks, databases, advanced features) based on user input (flags or interactive UI).

2. Top-level architectural components  
   a. User Interface Layer  
      • CLI entry point (main.go + cmd/root.go)  
      • Interactive UI components (cmd/ui/*) for multi-input, multi-select, spinner, text input  
      • Flag definitions (cmd/flags/*)  
   b. Command Orchestration Layer  
      • Command handlers (cmd/create.go, cmd/steps/steps.go)  
      • Program logic (cmd/program/program.go, cmd/program/*)  
      • Global config (cmd/globalEnv.go, cmd/version.go)  
   c. Template Engine Layer  
      • Template definitions (cmd/template/*) organized by feature:  
         – Frameworks (cmd/template/framework/*)  
         – Database drivers (cmd/template/dbdriver/*)  
         – Advanced features (HTMX, CI/CD, React, Tailwind, Docker) (cmd/template/advanced/*)  
      • File templating logic (go’s text/template under the hood)  
   d. Utility Layer  
      • Common helpers and abstractions (cmd/utils/*)  
   e. Output Layer  
      • Filesystem operations to write project directories and files  
      • Git initialization (optional “--git commit” integration)  

3. Relationships and data flows  
   1. User invokes `go-blueprint create [--flags]`  
   2. Root command parses flags, invokes interactive UI if needed  
   3. UI returns structured input (project name, framework, driver, advanced features)  
   4. Command orchestrator builds a plan (list of steps)  
   5. For each step:  
      a. Template Engine picks the right template based on input  
      b. Template is rendered with placeholders (project name, package names, imports)  
      c. Filesystem writer dumps the rendered files into a new project folder  
      d. Optionally invokes Git, Docker, or CI/CD setup routines  
   6. CLI reports success/failure  

4. Architectural patterns and design principles  
   - Layered architecture: UI → Orchestration → Templating → I/O  
   - Single binary with clearly separated packages (cmd, ui, template, utils)  
   - Template-driven code generation (declarative file templates)  
   - Dependency inversion: high-level CLI logic depends on abstract template interfaces  
   - Modularity: each feature (framework, driver, advanced) is a self-contained subpackage  

5. Tailoring the diagram  
   Since this is a CLI tool, emphasize:  
   - Input paths (flags vs. interactive UI)  
   - Core “create” command flow  
   - Template repository structure (show sub-directories for frameworks, db drivers, advanced features)  
   - File output and post-processing (Git, CI/CD, Docker)  
   - External integrations (HTTP frameworks, DB drivers) as “plug-in” boxes  

6. Diagramming guidelines  
   - Use distinct boxes for each layer:  
     • UI Layer (green)  
     • Command Orchestration (blue)  
     • Template Engine (orange)  
     • Output/Filesystem (gray)  
     • Utilities (yellow)  
   - Draw directional arrows to show flow:  
     User → CLI entry → Flag/UI parser → Orchestrator → Template Engine → Filesystem  
   - Represent template repositories as “folder” icons under the Template Engine box, labeled by feature  
   - Show optional paths (Git init, Docker, CI/CD) with dashed arrows  
   - Label every arrow with the data passed (e.g., “UserInput”, “RenderRequest”, “GeneratedFiles”)  
   - Use color-coded shapes:  
     – Rounded rectangles for packages/modules  
     – Cylinders for storage-like components (template directories, file system)  
     – Clouds or external icons for third-party frameworks and drivers  

7. Essential elements to include  
   - Clear component names (cmd/root, cmd/create, cmd/ui, cmd/template/advanced, etc.)  
   - Data-flow arrows with annotations  
   - Color legend for layers  
   - Notes on major external dependencies (Gin, Chi, Postgres, Mongo, Tailwind, React, etc.)  
   - A “New Project Output” box showing the generated project directory tree  

By following these guidelines, you'll produce a detailed, accurate system design diagram that clearly communicates how go-blueprint processes user input to generate a scaffolded Go project with optional integrations.  
</explanation>
